2026-08: Mixed. Public-facing momentum is genuinely strong — 26 openings in 2025, 30+ agreements signed for 2026, the Filakan three-unit NY/NJ deal, and an average operator owning 2+ locations, with no litigation or franchisee-association activity surfacing this cycle. But the 2025 FDD's own Item 19 shows FY2024 average adjusted EBITDA down 14.1% on flat revenue, at least one reporting unit at negative EBITDA, and the low occupancy reading falling from 59% to 53%. The August 2026 launch of the $492K Parlor format is itself corporate acknowledgment that the traditional $1.3M buildout had become too capital-heavy to recruit against, and 2026 franchisee-facing content is disproportionately focused on occupancy and lease-up — suggesting tenant recruitment is the live operator pain point.

## Investment Thesis

**Phenix Salon Suites** carries a **HOLD** signal with a FutureScore of 68/100. A salon-suite real-estate play that is fundamentally a landlord business: franchisees build 30-35 suites and rent them to independent beauty professionals at $250-$650+/week, with occupancy averaging 90% (median 94%) across 243 reporting units. The fee structure is genuinely operator-friendly — a fixed $0.34/sq ft royalty plus a $0.06/sq ft brand fee rather than percentage-of-revenue, so all revenue upside accrues to the owner — though a mandatory $1,000/month local advertising spend means the system is not fee-free, and the 'no ad fund' claim previously carried here was wrong. The Item 19 is unusually transparent and tells a cautionary story: FY2024 average gross revenue $474,101 with average adjusted EBITDA $150,178 (median $129,436), down 14.1% from FY2023 on flat revenue as margins compressed from 36.7% to 31.7%. That matters because the traditional format costs $1.2-1.42M to build and median EBITDA does not cover debt service on a fully financed unit — this is a low-leverage or all-cash play, not an SBA-maximised one. Scale drives everything: units over 6,000 sq ft average $709K revenue versus $333K under 4,500 sq ft. In August 2026 Phenix launched the sub-3,000 sq ft 'Parlor' format at roughly $492,000 average investment to attack exactly this capital barrier — the right strategic move, but it pushes new operators into the FDD's lowest-earning footprint band. Momentum is real, but Phenix ranks No. 132 on the 2026 Franchise 500 while Sola (750+ units) holds No. 1 in category and MY SALON Suite has grown past 370.

**Ideal Investor Profile:** A real-estate-experienced, low-leverage or all-cash buyer targeting large-format sites (6,000+ sq ft, where the FDD shows $709K average revenue), or an existing multi-unit Phenix operator using the new Parlor format for territory infill. Poor fit: a single-unit buyer maximising SBA leverage on a traditional build, since median adjusted EBITDA of $129,436 does not cover roughly $155,000 of annual debt service on a $1.0M note.

### Strengths

Fixed per-square-foot royalty ($0.34/sq ft) instead of percentage-of-revenue — every dollar of revenue upside above the fixed fee accrues to the operator, a structure almost unique in franchising2025 FDD Item 19 is one of the most detailed in the category — six parts covering gross revenue (average, median, high, low, top and bottom half), revenue distribution bands, adjusted EBITDA by year-opened cohort, occupancy for 2023 and 2024, and operating results cross-tabbed by square-footage bandOccupancy is genuinely high and stable: 243 reporting locations averaged 90% in both 2023 and 2024, with the median rising from 93% to 94%1-3 staff needed — the operating model is landlord-like and semi-absentee friendlyNew Phenix Parlor format (launched 2026-08-06) cuts average total investment to roughly $492,000 against ~$1.3M for a traditional location, directly attacking the capital-intensity problem that has been the model's core weakness

### Risk Factors

FY2024 average adjusted EBITDA fell 14.1% ($174,885 to $150,178) on flat revenue, compressing margin 5.0 points from 36.7% to 31.7% — rent, utilities and insurance are eating the suite-rental spreadMedian adjusted EBITDA of $129,436 does NOT cover roughly $155,000 of annual debt service on a $1.0M SBA note — a leveraged median-performing traditional unit is cash-flow negativeOnly 39.9% of eligible franchisees (134 of 336) reported financials for Item 19, so disclosed averages likely flatter the systemFranchised-unit growth decelerated to +3.1% in FY2024 (356 to 367) while the franchisor added +13 company-owned units — more than its franchisees addedThe new Parlor format steers buyers into the sub-4,500 sq ft band that the FDD's own data shows earns the least ($333,447 revenue, $88,696 adjusted EBITDA)

### How much does a Phenix Salon Suites franchise cost in 2026?

### What is the average AUV of a Phenix Salon Suites franchise?

The median Average Unit Volume (AUV) for Phenix Salon Suites franchises is $426K based on FDD Item 19 data across 425 US locations.

### How much do Phenix Salon Suites franchise owners make?

Typical Phenix Salon Suites owner earnings are approximately $75K per year, calculated from the median AUV ($426K) and a 17.5% net profit margin typical for the beauty & salon category. The realistic range for owner-operators is $63K to $86K per year depending on location and execution. For context, the median across the 98 franchises we track is $135K — Phenix Salon Suites sits below it, in the 16th percentile.

### What is the royalty rate for a Phenix Salon Suites franchise?

Phenix Salon Suites charges a 0.3% royalty on gross sales, for a total ongoing fee burden of 0.3% of revenue. This is disclosed in FDD Item 6.

### How long does it take to pay back a Phenix Salon Suites franchise?

The typical payback period for a Phenix Salon Suites franchise is 4-6 years based on median unit economics (AUV, owner earnings, and total investment). Top-quartile operators can pay back faster; bottom-quartile operators take significantly longer or never reach profitability.

### Is Phenix Salon Suites a good franchise to buy in 2026?

Our independent rating for Phenix Salon Suites is HOLD with a FutureScore of 68/100 based on 60+ data points. A salon-suite real-estate play that is fundamentally a landlord business: franchisees build 30-35 suites and rent them to independent beauty professionals at $250-$650+/week, with occupancy averaging 90% (median 94%) across 243 reporting units. The fee structure is genuinely operator-friendly — a fixed $0.34/sq ft royalty plus a $0.06/sq ft brand fee rather than percentage-of-revenue, so all revenue upside accrues to the owner — though a mandatory $1,000/month local advertising spend means the system is not fee-free, and the 'no ad fund' claim previously carried here was wrong. The Item 19 is unusually transparent and tells a cautionary story: FY2024 average gross revenue $474,101 with average adjusted EBITDA $150,178 (median $129,436), down 14.1% from FY2023 on flat revenue as margins compressed from 36.7% to 31.7%. That matters because the traditional format costs $1.2-1.42M to build and median EBITDA does not cover debt service on a fully financed unit — this is a low-leverage or all-cash play, not an SBA-maximised one. Scale drives everything: units over 6,000 sq ft average $709K revenue versus $333K under 4,500 sq ft. In August 2026 Phenix launched the sub-3,000 sq ft 'Parlor' format at roughly $492,000 average investment to attack exactly this capital barrier — the right strategic move, but it pushes new operators into the FDD's lowest-earning footprint band.
